title: Anything That Can Go Wrong, Will
hook: A split trash bag behind the bike shed tells Ivo his neat new rule has already learned to backfire.
counterintuition: A clean rule can become a dirty instruction once rewards touch it. The real test is not what the plan says, but what shortcut it makes rational.
tryThisNow: Before changing one rule, write the behavior it will reward, the shortcut it may invite, and the future cost it could hide. Fix the worst failure path first.
keyTakeaway: Judge a rule by the behavior it will create under pressure, then design guardrails for incentives, workarounds, and delayed costs before the rule goes live.

breakdown.fastRead:
Ivo stands over coffee grounds leaking from a split trash bag at 6:22 p.m. The new pay-per-bag rule did reduce bags at the curb. It also moved garbage behind the bike shed. A rule is not judged by its wording. It is judged by the behavior it creates.

When something can go wrong, the useful move is not panic. Trace the path. What does the metric reward? How might people adapt? What cost appears later? The fix that ignores those questions may become part of the problem.
breakdown.deepRead:
Galen writes "closed tickets" on the support-floor bonus board at 7:41 in the morning. The marker squeaks, and three agents glance up. Faster closure sounds clean. Customers hate waiting. But Galen can already picture the failure path: rushed replies, reopened tickets, hard cases pushed aside until the number looks good.

Incentives are not side notes. They are instructions. People tend to serve what the system pays, praises, or punishes. That is why a narrow metric can quietly replace the mission. If ticket count becomes survival, ticket count becomes the work.

Fariha sees the same pattern in a school attendance campaign. Perfect-month certificates looked harmless until feverish students sat in algebra coughing into sleeves. Atlanta high-stakes testing culture is the harder warning: when score pressure became the rewarded target, adults corrected student answers instead of protecting learning. The visible win hid a cost the dashboard did not count.

A better fix starts before launch. Ask what a tired, scared, ambitious, or rushed person will do with the rule. Ask what shortcut now becomes rational. Ask what looks better this month while making next month weaker. Then add guardrails, change the measure, or choose a different rule.
breakdown.fullRead:
Marisol stands by press line three at 5:55 in the morning with orange lockout tags spread across the table. Maintenance hours look easy to cut because they are quiet when they work. Her quarterly report will look cleaner if she trims two Friday crews. The machines will still run this week. That is why the choice is tempting.

Short-termism often wears a practical face. It improves the period being judged while moving the bill into the period nobody is staring at yet. The danger is not that every savings plan is foolish. The danger is that the visible number arrives before the hidden cost. A press that skips service can run fine Monday and fail in July.

Murphy's Law is useful when it is treated as design advice. If a failure path exists, assume the system will find it under pressure. That pressure may be fear, fatigue, ambition, boredom, money, status, or one impossible deadline. A rule that looks clean in a calm room can change shape on the floor.

Nello watches the curb at Alder and Ninth after a new no-loading sign goes up. The delivery vans do not vanish. They idle on side streets, block driveways, and make bicyclists swerve around them. The city solved the visible block and created three smaller ones nearby. That is the cobra effect in ordinary clothes: the remedy feeds a version of the problem because the system adapts.

Perverse incentives work the same way. A hospital that rewards speed alone may teach staff to move easy cases first. A school that rewards attendance alone may draw sick children into class. The phrase hospital and college rankings names the same pressure when rank becomes the target instead of a rough signal of quality. The measure has become a magnet.

A useful rule carries its own abuse case. If nobody can say how the rule might be gamed, the room has not finished thinking.

Ask the unpleasant question while the plan is still cheap to change. What will a reasonable person do if this target becomes their survival score? What will a rushed person skip? What will a clever person exploit? A plan that cannot survive those questions is not ready for people.

Tovah changes her clinic reminders after watching no-show penalties fail. The old rule charged patients who missed appointments. It felt fair and still left empty chairs. The new design sends bilingual texts, lets patients confirm with one tap, and calls the day before for rideshare-sensitive visits. She stops punishing the outcome and starts removing the failure path.

Before you launch a fix, run the adaptation test. Who is rewarded? Who is squeezed? What shortcut becomes attractive? What future cost becomes easier to ignore? What does the system do when nobody is watching the speech and everyone is watching the score? A strong rule survives those questions better than a neat rule. It works because it has already made room for human response.

examples.title: Galen pauses before writing closed tickets

planSpec.stakes: a narrow bonus could make service look faster while making customers worse off
planSpec.requiredBeat: he sees that rewarding closed tickets alone will invite rushed replies and decides whether to launch the metric

examples.scenario: The marker squeaks in Galen's hand at 7:41 a.m. on the Ellery Support floor as he writes "closed tickets" across the bonus board. Two agents are still eating granola bars at their desks. The metric will make the weekly chart simple, but he can already picture hard refunds being parked and easy password resets raced through. His thumb smears the wet ink. He has to decide whether speed alone is the number to pay for.
examples.whatToDo: Rewrite the metric before launch. Pair closure speed with reopened-ticket rate, customer notes, and a review of hard cases so the bonus rewards solved work, not hidden work.
examples.whyItMatters: A score becomes a set of instructions. If the system pays only for closed tickets, agents can serve the number while the customer problem keeps moving.

examples.title: Fariha counts cough drops beside perfect attendance

planSpec.stakes: a reward campaign may improve attendance while harming health and learning
planSpec.requiredBeat: she finds that the reward pulled sick students into class and hurt learning

examples.scenario: Cough drops spill beside Fariha's attendance charts at Friday 4:08 p.m. in the nurse's office. The perfect-month campaign worked on paper: absences fell 18 percent. The nurse's log tells the other half. Fever calls rose, two teachers lost review days, and one parent wrote that her son begged to come sick for the pizza party. Fariha circles the award column and sees the rule she built.
examples.whatToDo: Review what the campaign rewarded in practice. Keep attendance as a signal, but exclude illness days, track classroom disruption, and stop making sick presence the winning move.
examples.whyItMatters: The campaign did not just measure behavior. It changed behavior. A better design rewards the real aim, learning, without pulling children into class when staying home is right.

examples.title: Ivo hears the bag fee leak downstairs

planSpec.stakes: a fee meant to reduce waste may move the mess out of sight
planSpec.requiredBeat: a tenant points out that charging per trash bag has moved garbage behind the bike shed

examples.scenario: "Smell that?" Petra asks at Wednesday 6:22 p.m. in the basement laundry room. A split trash bag by the washer leaks coffee grounds into the floor drain. Ivo has just posted the new two-dollar curb bag fee to cut waste. Petra points toward the bike shed window. "The curb is cleaner because everyone is hiding bags back there." Ivo has the violation notices in his pocket and has to decide whether another penalty fixes this.
examples.whatToDo: Map the workaround before adding punishment. Check where the trash moved, why the fee made hiding rational, and whether shared bins or pickup changes would remove the dodge.
examples.whyItMatters: The first rule changed the path, not the problem. A second penalty may push the mess somewhere else unless the design makes the desired behavior easier.

examples.title: Marisol sees the quiet cost wake up

planSpec.stakes: maintenance cuts can improve one report while creating future downtime
planSpec.requiredBeat: she predicts a cleaner quarter, then sees downtime climb the next month

examples.scenario: Orange lockout tags lie on the table by press line three at Monday 5:55 a.m. Marisol's March forecast looked better after she cut two maintenance Fridays. She predicted a clean quarter and got it. Now April's first shift is silent while mechanics open the feeder housing. The supervisor does not say I told you so. He just hands her the downtime sheet, and Marisol has to decide whether the saved hours were real or only moved into lost production.
examples.whatToDo: Compare the savings across the full repair cycle, not just the reporting window. Restore maintenance where skipped work raises later downtime, and label those hours as capacity protection.
examples.whyItMatters: Some costs stay invisible until after the reward period. Short-term savings can be real and still be a bad trade if they drain the system that creates output.

examples.title: Nello watches vans reappear on Alder Street

planSpec.stakes: a clean curb rule may displace congestion rather than reduce it
planSpec.requiredBeat: he notices the system adapting around a clean rule

examples.scenario: A diesel van idles under the new no-loading sign at Alder and Ninth at Thursday 3:17 p.m., then rolls thirty yards and blocks a driveway. Nello stands with a folded curb map and watches two more vans copy it. The avenue looks clear in the enforcement photo. The side street smells like exhaust and wet cardboard. Nello must decide whether another sign fixes deliveries or only teaches them a new hiding place.
examples.whatToDo: Observe where the activity moved before declaring success. Redesign loading zones around real delivery needs, enforcement timing, and side-street spillover.
examples.whyItMatters: A system adapts around simple commands. If the measured spot improves while nearby streets absorb the cost, the policy has moved the problem rather than solved it.

examples.title: Tovah replaces penalties with one-tap reminders

planSpec.stakes: punishment may miss the cause of missed appointments
planSpec.requiredBeat: she shifts from punishing no-shows to removing the failure path that created them

examples.scenario: Postcard reminders sit in a plastic tray at Tuesday 10:36 a.m. on the Hillbend Clinic front desk. Before, Tovah mailed warnings and charged no-show fees. Empty chairs stayed empty. After three calls with patients, she changes the path: bilingual text reminders, one-tap confirmation, and a ride call for dialysis visits. The next missed slot will be tracked, but the first move is no longer punishment.
examples.whatToDo: Find the failure path before raising the penalty. Make confirmation easy, remove obvious access barriers, and reserve fees for cases where reminders and support already worked.
examples.whyItMatters: Punishment can feel fair while leaving the cause untouched. Removing the path to failure gives patients a better way to comply before the clinic counts them as careless.

questions.prompt: A sales team pays bonuses only for new accounts. Six weeks later, renewals are neglected and account managers avoid hard service calls. What should the leader change first?
choices: Add renewal health to the reward system so the metric matches the real aim.
Tell the team to care more about renewals while keeping the bonus unchanged.
Remove all metrics because people respond badly to measurement.
questions.explanation: The bonus is shaping behavior. If renewals matter, the system has to reward them instead of hoping a speech beats the visible incentive.

questions.prompt: A cafeteria bans snacks from classrooms. Wrappers disappear from desks but pile up in lockers and hallway vents by Friday. What does this show?
choices: The ban solved the real problem.
The behavior adapted around the rule and moved out of sight.
Students no longer want snacks.
questions.explanation: The visible measure improved while the underlying behavior shifted location. That is a warning to inspect the whole system, not just the monitored spot.

questions.prompt: A director cuts training to meet this quarter's budget, then quality defects rise two months later when new operators rotate onto the line. What model best explains the mistake?
choices: Short-termism, because the visible gain hid a later capability cost.
First principles, because the director started from basic truths.
Network effects, because each trainee increased the system's value.
questions.explanation: The budget looked better first, while the cost arrived later as defects. The mistake was judging the cut inside too narrow a time window.

questions.prompt: A town pays residents for each rat tail delivered, hoping to reduce the pest problem. Soon residents start breeding rats behind shops. What should a policy designer learn?
choices: Pay more per tail to clear the problem faster.
Cancel all public health programs.
Check whether the reward makes the harmful behavior profitable.
questions.explanation: The reward made the measured output valuable. A policy that pays for evidence of a problem can create more of the problem if adaptation is ignored.

questions.prompt: A manager wants to reduce errors by punishing every reported mistake in a lab handoff system. Which risk should she inspect before launch?
choices: Whether people will hide errors to avoid punishment.
Whether the punishment sounds strict enough in the memo.
Whether the error rate looks small this week.
questions.explanation: Punishing reports can make the dashboard cleaner while making the system more dangerous. The design must reward surfacing problems, not hiding them.

questions.prompt: A team adds a response-time target for customer support agents after complaints about delays. What guardrail would best prevent metric capture?
choices: A second measure for whether the answer actually solved the case.
A brighter dashboard that updates every hour.
A rule that agents must never question the target.
questions.explanation: A quality guardrail keeps speed from becoming the whole job. It makes the metric serve the goal instead of replacing it.

questions.prompt: A neighborhood rule clears scooters from one plaza, but by the next week they block the library entrance instead. What should be measured next?
choices: Only the original plaza, since that was the official target.
How the total scooter pattern changed across nearby spaces.
Whether residents remember the rule wording.
questions.explanation: The rule may have displaced the problem. Measuring nearby spaces shows whether the system improved or only moved the cost.

questions.prompt: A school wants higher test scores and considers rewards for teachers whose classes improve fastest on the spring exam. What question should come before launch?
choices: How can the fastest teachers be praised publicly?
What behavior might the reward create if scores become survival?
How can low-scoring students be removed from testing?
questions.explanation: High-stakes metrics can invite distorted behavior. The design should ask how people may serve the score instead of the learning.

questions.prompt: A clinic keeps charging missed-visit fees, but no-shows do not fall and the same patients keep missing early appointments. Which next move fits best?
choices: Raise the fee until missed visits become impossible.
Accept no-shows as a permanent market failure.
Trace the missed-visit path and remove barriers before increasing punishment.
questions.explanation: If punishment is not changing behavior, the failure path may be access, reminders, transport, or confusion. Fixing the path can work where pressure does not.

reviewCards.front: A new metric looks clean. What should you inspect before trusting it?
reviewCards.back: Inspect the behavior it rewards under pressure. A metric can start as measurement and become instruction once pay, praise, or punishment attaches to it.

reviewCards.front: A rule improves the monitored spot while trouble rises nearby. What is the likely failure?
reviewCards.back: The system adapted around the rule. Measure the whole pattern, including spillover, before calling the fix successful.

reviewCards.front: A cost cut helps this month and harms next quarter. What question should have been asked?
reviewCards.back: Ask what future capability the savings may drain. Short-termism hides damage by placing the reward and the bill in different time windows.

reviewCards.front: A punishment feels fair but does not reduce the behavior. What move comes next?
reviewCards.back: Trace the failure path. Find the shortcut, barrier, or workaround that makes the unwanted behavior rational, then redesign that path before adding more pressure.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is reading a rule as a system, not a sentence. Look for incentives, workarounds, spillover, and delayed costs before you trust the first visible improvement.

ifThenPlans.plan: If I introduce a metric, then I will write the three behaviors it may reward by accident and add at least one guardrail before launch.
If I set a strict personal rule, then I will ask how I might dodge it when tired and design the environment to make the better path easier.
If a quick fix saves money or time today, then I will check what maintenance, sleep, trust, or capacity it may cost next month.
If I use a threat to change someone's behavior, then I will ask what hiding, avoidance, or resentment the threat could reward.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, choose one rule, metric, or habit you rely on. Write the behavior it rewards, the easiest workaround, and one delayed cost, then adjust the rule to reduce the worst failure path.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, review one decision each day by asking: what did this reward, where did the problem move, and what cost might arrive later?

memorableLines.text: A rule is not judged by its wording.
memorableLines.why: It states the systems lens in a sentence readers can reuse.
It makes the hidden force feel central and urgent.

memorableLines.text: A strong rule survives those questions better than a neat rule.
memorableLines.why: It gives a clear test for policy quality.
